english.heading: Small Livestock Integration
body: Small livestock integration turns chickens, ducks, and bees into working parts of the farm.
Learn how animals can control pests, build fertility, support pollination, and return value to the soil.
Use the system you already have: food, manure, flowers, grazing, and careful movement across the land.

heading.text: Kopanyo ya Diphoofolo tse Nyenyane

body.text: Ho kopanya diphoofolo tse nyenyane tse ruuwang polasing ho etsa hore dikgoho (chickens), dipidipidi (ducks) le dinotshi (bees) di be dikarolo tse sebetsang tsa polasi.
body.backTranslation: Integrating small animals kept on the farm so that chickens (chickens), ducks (ducks) and bees (bees) become working parts of the farm.

body.text: Ithute hore diphoofolo di ka laola dikokwanyana tse senyang, tsa nontsha mobu, tsa thusa pollination, tsa kgutlisetsa boleng mobung.
body.backTranslation: Learn that animals can control insects that damage, and enrich the soil, and help pollination, and return quality to the soil.

body.text: Sebedisa tsamaiso eo o seng o e na le yona: dijo, manyolo, dipalesa, ho fula le ho suthisa diphoofolo ka hloko naheng.
body.backTranslation: Use the system you already have: food, manure, flowers, grazing and carefully moving animals on the land.

english.heading: Why This Matters
body: Small livestock can do work beyond producing meat, eggs, or honey.
Chickens eat some insects and weed seeds. Their manure can become compost.
Ducks scratch less than chickens, but can still damage plants.
Bees and other pollinators help many crops. Each animal still needs suitable food, water, shelter and care.

heading.text: Hobaneng Sena Se Bohlokwa

body.text: Diphoofolo tse nyenyane tse ruuwang di ka etsa mesebetsi e meng ntle le ho hlahisa nama, mahe kapa mahe a dinotshi.
body.backTranslation: Small animals that are kept can do other jobs besides producing meat, eggs or honey (lit. 'eggs of bees').

body.text: Dikgoho (chickens) di ja dikokwanyana tse ding le dipeo tsa dimela tse sa batleheng (weeds). Manyolo a tsona a ka fetoha compost.
body.backTranslation: Chickens (chickens) eat some insects and seeds of unwanted plants (weeds). Their manure can become compost.

body.text: Dipidipidi (ducks) ha di fate haholo jwaloka dikgoho (chickens), empa di ntse di ka senya dimela.
body.backTranslation: Ducks (ducks) do not scratch as much as chickens (chickens), but they can still damage plants.

body.text: Dinotshi (bees) le pollinators tse ding di thusa dijalo tse ngata. Phoofolo e nngwe le e nngwe e ntse e hloka dijo tse loketseng, metsi, setshabelo le tlhokomelo.
body.backTranslation: Bees (bees) and other pollinators help many crops. Each and every animal still needs suitable food, water, shelter and care.

english.heading: Learning Outcomes
body: By the end of this module, you will understand how chickens, ducks, bees, and guinea fowl fit into a working system.
You will know when chickens help a bed, and when their scratching can cause damage.
You will understand pollination, hive placement, and how livestock move nutrients around a farm.

heading.text: Dipheo tsa Ho Ithuta

body.text: Qetellong ya module ena, o tla utlwisisa hore dikgoho (chickens), dipidipidi (ducks), dinotshi (bees) le guinea fowl di kena jwang tsamaisong e sebetsang.
body.backTranslation: By the end of this module, you will understand how chickens (chickens), ducks (ducks), bees (bees) and guinea fowl fit into a working system.

body.text: O tla tseba hore dikgoho (chickens) di thusa bethe ya dijalo (bed) neng, le hore ho fata ha tsona ho ka baka tshenyo neng.
body.backTranslation: You will know when chickens (chickens) help the crop bed (bed), and when their scratching can cause damage.

body.text: O tla utlwisisa pollination, moo hive e behwang teng, le hore diphoofolo di tsamaisa nutrients polasing jwang.
body.backTranslation: You will understand pollination, where a hive is placed, and how animals move nutrients on the farm.

english.heading: Watch: Hens Foraging After Harvest
body: Watch the hens peck at the ground among dry plant remains.
Chickens may eat some insects and weed seeds. They still need balanced feed, clean water and shelter.
Keep them away from seedlings and food ready to harvest.

heading.text: Sheba: Dikgoho Di Batla Dijo Kamora Kotulo
heading.backTranslation: Look: Chickens Look for Food After Harvest

body.text: Sheba dikgoho tse tshehadi (hens) di kgotha (peck) fatshe hara masalla a dimela a omileng.
body.backTranslation: Watch the hens (hens) peck (peck) on the ground among dry plant remains.

body.text: Dikgoho (chickens) di ka ja dikokwanyana tse ding le dipeo tsa dimela tse sa batleheng (weeds). Di ntse di hloka dijo tsa diphoofolo tse leka-lekaneng, metsi a hlwekileng le setshabelo.
body.backTranslation: Chickens (chickens) can eat some insects and seeds of unwanted plants (weeds). They still need adequate animal feed, clean water and shelter.

body.text: Di boloke hole le dimela tse ntjha (seedlings) le dijo tse seng di loketse ho kotulwa.
body.backTranslation: Keep them away from young plants (seedlings) and food that is ready to be harvested.

english.heading: Chickens Turn Scratching Into Useful Work
body: Chickens can help an empty bed after harvest.
They scratch through plant remains and eat some insects and weed seeds.
Their manure and bedding can be composted and returned to the soil.
Foraging does not replace a balanced diet, clean water, shelter or daily care.

heading.text: Ho Ngwapa ha Dikgoho ke Mosebetsi o Thusang

body.text: Dikgoho (chickens) di ka thusa bethe ya dijalo e se nang letho kamora kotulo.
body.backTranslation: Chickens (chickens) can help an empty bed of crops after harvest.

body.text: Di fata hara masalla a dimela mme di ja dikokwanyana tse ding le dipeo tsa dimela tse sa batleheng (weeds).
body.backTranslation: They scratch among the plant remains and eat some insects and the seeds of unwanted plants (weeds).

body.text: Manyolo a tsona le bedding di ka etswa compost mme tsa kgutlisetswa mobung.
body.backTranslation: Their manure and bedding can be made into compost and returned to the soil.

body.text: Ho batla dijo ha ho nke sebaka sa dijo tsa diphoofolo tse leka-lekaneng, metsi a hlwekileng, setshabelo kapa tlhokomelo ya letsatsi le letsatsi.
body.backTranslation: Looking for food does not take the place of adequate animal feed, clean water, shelter or daily care.

english.heading: Use Chickens at the Right Time
body: Use chickens in an empty bed after harvest.
Keep them away from seedlings and crops being harvested for food.
Fresh manure can carry germs. Ask an extension adviser how to manage manure safely before the next crop.
Move the birds before they damage the ground.

heading.text: Sebedisa Dikgoho Nakong e Nepahetseng
heading.backTranslation: Use Chickens at the Right Time

body.text: Sebedisa dikgoho (chickens) bething ya dijalo e se nang letho kamora kotulo.
body.backTranslation: Use chickens (chickens) in a bed of crops that is empty after harvest.

body.text: Di boloke hole le dimela tse ntjha (seedlings) le dijalo tse kotulwang bakeng sa dijo.
body.backTranslation: Keep them away from young plants (seedlings) and crops being harvested for food.

body.text: Manyolo a ntjha a ka jara dikokwanahloko tse bakang malwetse (germs). Botsa extension adviser hore na o ka tsamaisa manyolo ka polokeho jwang pele ho jalo e latelang.
body.backTranslation: Fresh manure can carry disease-causing germs. Ask an extension adviser how you can handle manure safely before the next crop.

body.text: Sisinya dinonyana pele di senya fatshe.
body.backTranslation: Move the birds before they damage the ground.

english.heading: Ducks Suit Established Understorey
body: Ducks eat slugs and snails without the heavy scratching of chickens.
They may suit an established food forest understorey.
They can still eat or trample plants and make wet ground muddy. Watch the birds and move them when needed.
Provide clean water and suitable feed; foraging alone may not be enough.

heading.text: Dipidipidi di Loketse Understorey e Tsepameng

body.text: Dipidipidi (ducks) di ja slugs le snails ntle le ho fata haholo jwalo ka dikgoho (chickens).
body.backTranslation: Ducks (ducks) eat slugs (slugs) and snails (snails) without scratching as much as chickens (chickens).

body.text: Di kanna tsa loketsa food forest understorey e thehilweng.
body.backTranslation: They may suit an established food forest understorey.

body.text: Di ntse di ka ja kapa di hatakela dimela, mme di ka etsa hore fatshe le metsi-metsi le be seretse. Shebisisa dinonyana mme o di suthise ha ho hlokeha.
body.backTranslation: They can still eat or trample plants, and can make the ground and wet places turn to mud. Watch the birds closely and move them when needed.

body.text: Fana ka metsi a hlwekileng le dijo tsa diphoofolo tse loketseng; ho batla dijo feela ho ka ba ho sa lekane.
body.backTranslation: Provide clean water and suitable animal feed; looking for food alone may not be enough.

english.heading: Rotate the Tractor Across the Plot
body: A chicken tractor is a moveable, floorless pen.
Move it before the ground becomes bare, muddy or heavily covered with manure.
The right time depends on the birds, soil and weather. Let the ground recover between visits.
There is no single number of chickens that guarantees enough fertility for every plot.

heading.text: Potoloha chicken tractor Sebakeng sa Dijalo
heading.backTranslation: Move the chicken tractor Around the Crop Area

body.text: Chicken tractor ke lesaka le ka suthiswang, le se nang mokato (floorless).
body.backTranslation: A chicken tractor is a movable pen without a floor (floorless).

body.text: Le suthise pele fatshe le fetoha le se nang letho, seretse kapa le kwahetswe haholo ke manyolo.
body.backTranslation: Move it before the ground becomes bare, muddy or heavily covered in manure.

body.text: Nako e nepahetseng e itshetlehile ka dinonyana, mobu le boemo ba lehodimo. Lesa fatshe le hlaphohelle pakeng tsa ketelo le ketelo.
body.backTranslation: The right timing depends on the birds, the soil and the weather. Let the ground rest and recover between each visit.

body.text: Ha ho na palo e le nngwe ya dikgoho (chickens) e netefatsang ho nontsha mobu ho lekaneng bakeng sa sebaka se seng le se seng sa dijalo.
body.backTranslation: There is no single number of chickens (chickens) that guarantees adequate fertilising of the soil for every crop area.

english.heading: Watch: A Bee Moves Between Two Blossoms
body: Watch one bee move from one blossom to another.
Bees can carry pollen as they visit flowers.

heading.text: Sheba: Notshi (bee) Pakeng tsa Dipalesa Tse Pedi
heading.backTranslation: Look: A Bee (bee) Between Two Flowers

body.text: Sheba notshi (bee) e le nngwe e tloha palesa e nngwe e ya ho e nngwe.
body.backTranslation: Look at one bee (bee) going from one flower to another.

body.text: Dinotshi (bees) di ka jara pollen ha di etela dipalesa.
body.backTranslation: Bees (bees) can carry pollen when they visit flowers.

english.heading: Bees Help Pollinate Many Crops
body: Honeybees and other insects carry pollen between flowers.
This helps many fruit and vegetable crops, including avocado. Different crops and varieties have different pollination needs.
A hive does not guarantee higher yields everywhere. Weather, water, plant health and other pollinators also matter.

heading.text: Dinotshi di Thusa Pollination ya Dijalo Tse Ngata
heading.backTranslation: Bees Help Pollination of Many Crops

body.text: Dinotshi (honeybees) le dikokwanyana tse ding di jara pollen pakeng tsa dipalesa.
body.backTranslation: Bees (honeybees) and other insects carry pollen between flowers.

body.text: Sena se thusa dijalo tse ngata tsa ditholwana le meroho, ho kenyeletswa avocado. Dijalo le mefuta (varieties) e fapaneng di na le ditlhoko tse fapaneng tsa pollination.
body.backTranslation: This helps many crops of fruits and vegetables, including avocado. Crops and different varieties (varieties) have different needs of pollination.

body.text: Hive ha e netefatse kotulo e phahameng hohle. Boemo ba lehodimo, metsi, bophelo bo botle ba dimela le pollinators tse ding le tsona di bohlokwa.
body.backTranslation: A hive does not guarantee a high harvest everywhere. The state of the sky, water, good health of plants and other pollinators also are important.

english.heading: South Africa’s Native Honeybees
body: South Africa has two native honeybee subspecies.
The Cape honeybee is found in the Western Cape and parts of the Eastern Cape. The African honeybee is native to central and most of southern Africa.
These broad natural ranges are not a guide for moving bees. The Department's control measures set a demarcation line for bee movement. Check current rules before moving bees or hives.

heading.text: Dinotshi (honeybees) tsa Tlhaho tsa Afrika Borwa

body.text: Afrika Borwa e na le subspecies tse pedi tsa dinotshi (honeybees) tsa tlhaho.
body.backTranslation: South Africa has two natural subspecies of honeybees (honeybees).

body.text: Cape honeybee e fumanwa Western Cape le dibakeng tse ding tsa Eastern Cape. African honeybee ke ya tlhaho bohareng ba Afrika le boholo ba borwa ba Afrika.
body.backTranslation: The Cape honeybee is found in the Western Cape and some areas of the Eastern Cape. The African honeybee is native to central Africa and most of southern Africa.

body.text: Dibaka tsena tse kgolo tsa tlhaho ha di a lokela ho sebediswa e le tataiso ya ho fallisa dinotshi (bees). Mehato ya taolo ya Lefapha (Department) e beha demarcation line bakeng sa ho fallisa dinotshi. Hlahloba melao ya hajwale pele o fallisa dinotshi kapa dihive.
body.backTranslation: These large natural areas should not be used as a guide for moving bees (bees). The control steps (measures) of the Department (Department) set a demarcation line for moving bees. Check the current laws before you move bees or hives.

english.heading: Place the Hive With Care
body: Learn from an experienced local beekeeper before getting a hive.
Keep hives away from busy paths, homes and places where children play.
Morning sun can help, but a safe location comes first.
Plan how people and animals will move around the site.

heading.text: Beha Hive ka Hloko

body.text: Ithute ho moboloki wa dinotshi (bees) wa sebakeng ya nang le phihlelo pele o fumana hive.
body.backTranslation: Learn from an experienced local beekeeper (bees) before you get a hive.

body.text: Boloka dihive hole le ditselana tse nang le batho ba bangata, matlo le dibaka moo bana ba bapalang teng.
body.backTranslation: Keep hives away from busy paths, houses and places where children play.

body.text: Letsatsi la hoseng le ka thusa, empa sebaka se sireletsehileng se tla pele.
body.backTranslation: Morning sun can help, but a safe place comes first.

body.text: Rera hore batho le diphoofolo ba tla tsamaya jwang ho potoloha sebaka.
body.backTranslation: Plan how people and animals will move around the place.

english.heading: Strong Colonies Need Care and Flowers
body: Provide flowering plants through the seasons and avoid exposing bees to pesticides.
Active bees do not prove that the farm is free of chemicals or disease.

Registration is required for activities defined by the national honey-bee control measures. These include keeping managed hives for bee products, queen rearing, commercial pollination, and removing, eradicating or relocating colonies. Check with the Department if you are unsure whether your activity is covered.
If a colony swarms repeatedly, ask a trained beekeeper to inspect it. Crowding is one possible cause, not a diagnosis.

heading.text: Dikolone Tse Matla: Tlhokomelo le Dipalesa

body.text: Fana ka dimela tse thehang dipalesa ka dinako tsohle tsa selemo mme o qobe ho pepesa dinotshi (bees) ho pesticides.
body.backTranslation: Provide plants that produce flowers at all times of the year and avoid exposing bees (bees) to pesticides.

body.text: Dinotshi (bees) tse sebetsang ha di fane ka bopaki ba hore polasi ha e na dikhemikhale kapa malwetse.
body.backTranslation: Active bees (bees) do not give proof that the farm has no chemicals or diseases.

body.text: Ngodiso (registration) e a hlokahala bakeng sa mesebetsi e hlalositsweng ke national honey-bee control measures. Mesebetsi ena e kenyeletsa ho boloka dihive tse laolwang bakeng sa dihlahiswa tsa dinotshi (bees), queen rearing, commercial pollination, le ho tlosa, ho fedisa kapa ho fallisa dikolone. Botsa Lefapha (Department) haeba o sa tsebe hore na mosebetsi wa hao o kenyeletswa.
body.backTranslation: Registration (registration) is needed for activities that are defined by national honey-bee control measures. These activities include keeping controlled hives for products of bees (bees), queen rearing, commercial pollination, and removing, finishing (ending) or moving colonies. Ask the Department (Department) if you do not know whether your work is included.

body.text: Haeba kolone e etsa swarm kgafetsa, kopa moboloki wa dinotshi (bees) ya kwetlisitsweng hore a e hlahlobe. Ho hloka sebaka ka hare ho hive (crowding) ke lebaka le le leng le ka bang teng, e seng diagnosis.
body.backTranslation: If a colony makes swarm repeatedly, ask a trained beekeeper of bees (bees) to inspect it. Lacking space inside the hive (crowding) is one possible reason, not a diagnosis.

english.heading: Nutrients Moving Through the Farm
body: Some nutrients move from plants to animals. Bought feed also brings nutrients into the farm. Some nutrients may return to the growing area through compost made from manure. Food and other products carry nutrients away.

heading.text: Nutrients di Tsamaya Polasing

body.text: Nutrients tse ding di tloha dimeleng di ya ho diphoofolo. Dijo tsa diphoofolo tse rekilweng le tsona di tlisa nutrients polasing. Nutrients tse ding di kanna tsa kgutlela sebakeng sa ho jala ka compost e entsweng ka manyolo. Dijo le dihlahiswa tse ding di jara nutrients di di tlosa.
body.backTranslation: Some nutrients go from plants to animals. Bought animal feed also brings nutrients onto the farm. Some nutrients may return to the planting area in compost made from manure. Food and other products carry nutrients away (remove them).

english.heading: Some Nutrients Return; Others Enter and Leave
body: Animals can return some nutrients through compost made from manure. Fresh manure can carry harmful germs. Compost manure fully before using it around food crops.
Chickens eat suitable farm produce and insects.
Bought feed brings nutrients into the farm. Food sold or taken home and other products carry nutrients away. Keep track of feed bought in and food sold or taken home.
Scraps alone may not meet the animals’ needs.

heading.text: Tse Ding Di Kgutla; Tse Ding Di Kena le Ho Tswa
heading.backTranslation: Some Return; Some Come In and Go Out

body.text: Diphoofolo di ka kgutlisa nutrients tse ding ka compost e entsweng ka manyolo. Manyolo a ntjha a ka jara dikokwanahloko tse kotsi (germs). Etsa compost ya manyolo ka ho feletseng pele o a sebedisa haufi le dijalo tsa dijo.
body.backTranslation: Animals can return some nutrients through compost made from manure. Fresh manure can carry harmful germs. Make manure compost completely before you use it near food crops.

body.text: Dikgoho (chickens) di ja dihlahiswa tse loketseng tsa polasi le dikokwanyana.
body.backTranslation: Chickens (chickens) eat suitable farm products and insects.

body.text: Dijo tsa diphoofolo tse rekilweng di kenya nutrients polasing. Dijo tse rekisitsweng kapa tse nkilweng ho ya hae le dihlahiswa tse ding di jara nutrients di di tlosa. Boloka rekoto ya dijo tsa diphoofolo tse rekilweng le dijo tse rekisitsweng kapa tse nkilweng ho ya hae.
body.backTranslation: Bought animal feed puts nutrients onto the farm. Food sold or taken home, and other products, carry nutrients away. Keep a record of animal feed bought and food sold or taken home.

body.text: Masalla a dijo feela a kanna a se ke a fihlella ditlhoko tsa diphoofolo.
body.backTranslation: Leftovers of food alone may not meet the needs of the animals.

english.heading: Guinea Fowl Forage, but Health Checks Still Matter
body: Guinea fowl forage for insects and may eat ticks.
Do not rely on them to protect people or livestock from ticks or tick-borne disease.
Keep checking animals and follow a local animal-health plan.
Foraging birds are one part of the farm, not a replacement for health care.

heading.text: Guinea Fowl di Iphepa, empa o Ntse o Hlahloba Bophelo
heading.backTranslation: Guinea Fowl Feed Themselves, but You Still Check Health

body.text: Guinea fowl di batla dikokwanyana mme di ka ja ticks.
body.backTranslation: Guinea fowl look for insects and can eat ticks.

body.text: O se ke wa di tshepa hore di sireletse batho kapa diphoofolo ho ticks kapa malwetse a jarwang ke ticks.
body.backTranslation: Do not trust them to protect people or animals from ticks or tick-borne diseases.

body.text: Tswela pele o hlahloba diphoofolo mme o latele morero wa sebakeng wa bophelo bo botle ba diphoofolo (animal-health plan).
body.backTranslation: Keep checking the animals and follow the local animal-health plan (animal-health plan).

body.text: Dinonyana tse batlang dijo ke karolo e le nngwe ya polasi, e sa nkeng sebaka sa tlhokomelo ya bophelo bo botle.
body.backTranslation: Birds that look for food are one part of the farm, which does not take the place of health care.

english.heading: Ask Three Questions for Every Animal
body: For each animal, ask what it can eat here.
Ask what useful things it produces.
Then ask what else it needs. Include water, suitable feed, shelter, fencing and daily care.
Some needs may require bought inputs. Plan for them before bringing animals onto the land.

heading.text: Dipotso Tse Tharo ka Phoofolo e Nngwe le e Nngwe

body.text: Bakeng sa phoofolo e nngwe le e nngwe, botsa hore na e ka ja eng mona.
body.backTranslation: For each animal, ask what it can eat here.

body.text: Botsa hore na e hlahisa dintho dife tse molemo.
body.backTranslation: Ask what good things it produces.

body.text: Ebe o botsa hore na e hloka eng hape. Kenyeletsa metsi, dijo tsa diphoofolo tse loketseng, setshabelo, terata (fencing) le tlhokomelo ya letsatsi le letsatsi.
body.backTranslation: Then ask what else it needs. Include water, suitable animal food, shelter, fencing (fencing) and daily care.

body.text: Ditlhoko tse ding di kanna tsa hloka inputs tse rekilweng. Di rerele pele o tlisa diphoofolo naheng.
body.backTranslation: Some needs may require bought inputs (inputs). Plan for them before you bring animals onto the land.

english.heading: Grazing and Goat Worm Control
body: Chickens following goats are not a proven replacement for goat worm control.
Grazing management can help, but goats still need health checks.
Work with a veterinary or animal-health adviser on a parasite plan for your herd.
Do not stop treatment because chickens have visited the grazing camp.

heading.text: Ho Fula le Taolo ya Diboko tsa Mala tsa Dipodi (goats)
heading.backTranslation: Grazing and Control of Worms of the Intestines of Goats (goats)

body.text: Dikgoho (chickens) tse latelang dipodi (goats) ha di a netefatswa hore di ka nka sebaka sa taolo ya diboko tsa mala (worms) tsa dipodi.
body.backTranslation: Chickens (chickens) that follow goats (goats) are not guaranteed to be able to replace the control of intestinal worms (worms) of goats.

body.text: Taolo ya ho fula e ka thusa, empa dipodi di ntse di hloka hlahlobo ya bophelo.
body.backTranslation: Grazing management can help, but goats still need a health check.

body.text: Sebetsa le ngaka ya diphoofolo kapa moeletsi wa bophelo ba diphoofolo ho rera morero wa parasites bakeng sa mohlape wa hao.
body.backTranslation: Work with a veterinarian or animal health adviser to plan a parasite plan for your herd.

body.text: O se ke wa emisa kalafo hobane dikgoho (chickens) di kile tsa kena kampong ya ho fula (grazing camp).
body.backTranslation: Do not stop treatment because chickens (chickens) have entered the grazing camp (grazing camp) at some point.

english.heading: Field Assignment: Draw Where Resources Go
body: Walk your smallholding and choose an area where livestock could support another part of the system.
Record what food, scraps, pests, surplus produce, manure, or flowering resources are already present.
Then note what each animal could produce, and what it would need from the farm.
Draw one useful link between livestock and the rest of your farm. Show what comes in and what leaves.

heading.text: Mosebetsi wa Naheng: Taka Hore Methopo e Ya Kae
heading.backTranslation: Field Task: Draw Where the Resources Go

body.text: Tsamaya polasing ya hao e nyenyane o kgethe sebaka seo diphoofolo di ka thusang karolo e nngwe ya tsamaiso.
body.backTranslation: Walk through your small farm and choose a place where animals could help one part of the system.

body.text: Ngola hore ke dijo, masalla, dikokwanyana tse senyang (pests), dihlahiswa tse setseng, manyolo kapa methopo ya dipalesa life tse seng di le teng.
body.backTranslation: Write down which food, leftovers, pests (pests), remaining products, manure or sources of flowers already exist.

body.text: Ebe o ngola hore phoofolo e nngwe le e nngwe e ka hlahisa eng, le hore e tla hloka eng polasing.
body.backTranslation: Then write down what each animal could produce, and what it will need on the farm.

body.text: Taka kamano e le nngwe e molemo pakeng tsa diphoofolo le karolo e setseng ya polasi ya hao. Bontsha se kenang le se tlohang.
body.backTranslation: Draw one good relationship between the animals and the remaining part of your farm. Show what comes in and what goes out.

english.heading: Field Action: Put One Link to Work
body: Choose one safe action from this module.
Plan how chickens could use an empty bed after harvest, ask a beekeeper about a safe hive position, or check your animals’ daily needs.
Record the food, water, shelter and care that the action requires.
Start with the resources and help you can reliably provide.

heading.text: Ketso ya Naheng: Sebedisa Kamano e le Nngwe

body.text: Kgetha ketso e le nngwe e sireletsehileng ho tswa moduleng ena.
body.backTranslation: Choose one safe action from this module.

body.text: Rera hore dikgoho (chickens) di ka sebedisa jwang bethe ya dijalo e se nang letho kamora kotulo, botsa moboloki wa dinotshi (bees) ka sebaka se sireletsehileng sa hive, kapa hlahloba ditlhoko tsa letsatsi le letsatsi tsa diphoofolo tsa hao.
body.backTranslation: Plan how chickens (chickens) could use an empty crop bed (bed) after harvest, ask a beekeeper (bees) about a safe hive location, or check the daily needs of your animals.

body.text: Ngola dijo, metsi, setshabelo le tlhokomelo tseo ketso eo e di hlokang.
body.backTranslation: Write down the food, water, shelter and care that the action requires.

body.text: Qala ka methopo le thuso tseo o ka di fanang ka tshepahalo.
body.backTranslation: Start with the resources and help that you can provide reliably.
